transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Nakamura, I have your final results from the CT scan we did yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, okay. I was reading on a forum that a CT angiogram can sometimes miss smaller clots, but the sensitivity is usually pretty high. Did it show the embolism?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It did. The scan showed a pulmonary embolism, which is a blood clot in your lung.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I knew it. I felt it in my chest. Why didn't you tell me yesterday? I was waiting for hours.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to be honest about what happened. There was a mistake. The clot was visible on the images, but the radiologist who did the preliminary read didn't include it in the report. Because of that, we didn't start your treatment for eighteen hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Eighteen hours? Wait, so the image was there, but the person reading it just... missed it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My god. I was lying there thinking I was just anxious. Was I in danger? While I was just sitting there waiting for you to come back?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry for the confusion and the delay. We were incredibly busy yesterday with several admissions, and the report didn't get flagged for a second look until the attending radiologist reviewed it this morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're sorry for the confusion? This isn't confusion, this is a missed diagnosis. I could have had another clot. I could have died.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that you're really scared right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Of course I'm scared! I'm twenty-three and I'm in a hospital bed because someone forgot to write something down in a report.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. Does that make sense so far, or can I clarify how the reporting process works?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I understand the process. You're saying the doctor looked at the picture, didn't see the clot, wrote the report, and then eighteen hours later another doctor looked at the same picture and saw it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How do I know the treatment you're giving me now is actually right? If you can miss a whole clot, what else did you miss?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. You've lost trust in us because of this delay. To make sure we are on the right track, I've already had the attending radiologist and the chief of pulmonary medicine double-check every single slice of your scan to confirm there are no other clots. They've both signed off on the current findings.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And now what? Do I just stay here and hope no one else forgets to read a chart?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is exactly what we are doing now. First, you are already on the Heparin drip, which prevents new clots from forming. We will keep you on that for the next five days. Second, I am scheduling a follow-up ultrasound for your legs tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to see if there's a source clot there. Third, I've entered a hard-stop alert in your electronic chart that requires a manual sign-off from the attending physician every twelve hours regarding your coagulation levels.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do I need to do?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your role is to monitor for any sudden increase in shortness of breath or chest pain. If you feel that, press the call button immediately. If you don't feel a change, you just need to stay in bed for the next twenty-four hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is this going to happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are filing a formal incident report today. This means the radiology department has to conduct a root-cause analysis to figure out why the preliminary read missed this and change their workflow so it doesn't happen to anyone else. I will bring you a copy of the report number so you can track the investigation if you want.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I can't believe I spent all night waiting for a report that was already finished.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it's incredibly frustrating. I really need to step out to check on another patient who is crashing, but I'll be back in twenty minutes to check your vitals. Do you have any other questions before I go?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. I just need to look at this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be back soon.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language at the end of the encounter ('I really need to step out to check on another patient who is crashing').

E.justification: The error is explicitly named in the second turn, lay language is used throughout, and comprehension is checked twice ('Does that make sense so far' and 'Do you have any other questions').

A.justification: While a direct apology is used, it is diluted by an excuse regarding being 'incredibly busy yesterday with several admissions.'

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions twice ('scared', 'frustrating') and references the patient's loss of trust.

T.justification: The resident provides specific steps with timelines (Heparin for 5 days, ultrasound tomorrow at 8 AM), defines the patient's role (monitor for shortness of breath), and addresses prevention (incident report/root-cause analysis).
